extracted.intended_audience: biomedical researchers, journal editors, research administrators, and research integrity officers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and lessons for preventing, detecting, and responding to research misconduct in biomedical fields, drawn from the Hwang stem-cell fraud case. Covers education, peer review, auditing, authorship, and institutional/international policy measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for international RCR guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: The research community needs international guidelines for RCR that define a set of ethical standards (or best practices) as well as procedures for interpreting and enforcing these standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidelines should include rules for protecting whistleblowers, maintaining confidentiality during investigations, and guaranteeing due process. Such standards could be established and promoted through the national science ministries of cooperating states to reduce inconsistency across countries.

rubrics_metrics.name: RCR education is important
rubrics_metrics.description: Education in the responsible conduct of research (RCR) raises awareness about ethical issues and how to address them, promotes an institutional culture of integrity, and is therefore important even though it will not prevent all misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: RCR education works best in interactive settings rather than purely online; current education rates are slow (may take decades to reach all researchers). Institutions and funders should expand and prioritize RCR training for students and researchers (NIH intramural program requires an initial online course and annual updates as an example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review is limited in detecting misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: The peer review process almost always fails to detect research misconduct because reviewers typically see only the manuscript and not underlying materials such as lab notebooks, biological samples, or instruments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers and editors should still be vigilant about novelty, significance, methodological soundness, data consistency, validity of analysis/interpretation, and quality of writing. Recognize peer review's limitations and consider supplementary checks or policies (e.g., data availability, post-publication review, access to underlying materials) to improve detection of fraud.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scrutinize images and photographic evidence for manipulation or duplication
rubrics_metrics.description: Identical photographs or unusually homologous electrophoresis images derived from different sources can be an indicator of fraud; careful examination of submitted photographs contributed to disclosures in the Hwang case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peer reviewers, journal editors, and staff should pay attention to photographs and digital images for evidence of tampering or improbable similarities. Journals should adopt strict image-manipulation policies (example: Journal of Cell Biology guidelines) and implement checks for duplicated or manipulated images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audit data and research records as quality control
rubrics_metrics.description: Auditing data and research records and materials is an effective quality-control measure to detect research misconduct before publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audits should occur for cause (suspected problems) and on a random basis; they should be limited in scope (estimated not to exceed ~1% of studies). Academic institutions should allocate resources for auditing, potentially include auditing costs in grant budgets, and normalize audits so they are not perceived as punitive. Audits help catch honest errors before submission and can benefit researchers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship accountability and contribution disclosure (ICMJE/JAMA policy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each author should have participated sufficiently to take public responsibility for appropriate portions of the content; one or more authors should take responsibility for the integrity of the work as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorship credit should be based only on (1) substantial contributions to conception/design, acquisition of data, or analysis/interpretation; (2) drafting or critical revision for important intellectual content; and (3) final approval of the version to be published — all three conditions must be met. Journals should require signed authorship forms stating contributions, financial disclosures, and copyright/transfer or employment status. Such policies promote accountability and discourage honorary authorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect against coercive recruitment of research subjects/donors
rubrics_metrics.description: The participation of subordinates in a supervisor's research (e.g., oocyte donation by junior lab members) is ethically problematic because it can be coercive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers and institutions should avoid recruiting donors who are in subordinate relationships to investigators and should scrutinize compensation practices (the Hwang case reported donors received up to $1,400). Ethical review and consent processes must guard against coercion and undue influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whistleblower protections and transparent investigation procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Whistleblowers often play a central role in uncovering misconduct; institutions must have procedures to protect them and to carry out fair investigations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigative procedures should include whistleblower protection, confidentiality protections during investigations, and guarantees of due process for those accused. Clear, pre-established procedures reduce ad-hoc reactions to scandals and help ensure fair outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional commitment to auditing and cultural change
rubrics_metrics.description: Academic institutions often resist auditing due to perceived costs, inconvenience to researchers, and fear of implying unethical behavior; this resistance undermines data quality control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions should allocate modest resources (auditing cost estimated at ≤1% of study cost), include auditing in grant or administrative budgets, educate researchers to accept occasional audits, and assure researchers that honest errors will not be punished. Normalizing audits will reduce intimidation and improve research integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial and coauthor responsibilities prior to submission
rubrics_metrics.description: Senior authors and editors have responsibilities to ensure the veracity of data, detect inconsistencies, and confirm that each coauthor has approved the manuscript prior to submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure of senior authors to verify data and secure coauthor approval (as in the Schatten example) constitutes research misbehavior. Journals should adopt policies requiring statements of contribution and author approval, and editors should be vigilant about unusual authorship arrangements and potential conflicts of interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require financial disclosure and conflict-of-interest transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorship forms and journal policies should require disclosure of financial interests and consulting fees that may influence research integrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signed statements on financial disclosure (as part of authorship submission) help surface potentially problematic relationships (e.g., unusually high consulting fees) and support assessment of biases. Journals and institutions should enforce disclosure requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize limits of peer review and enable access to underlying materials when needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Because peer reviewers normally lack access to lab notebooks, samples, and instruments, detecting some forms of misconduct requires access to these materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies that permit or require access to underlying data/materials for investigations or enhanced review (e.g., upon suspicion) improve the ability to detect fabrication/falsification. Consider practices like data deposition, availability on request, or licensing limited access for verification.
